evidence.excerpt: Once a finite automaton model of a protocol is inferred from normal traffic, it can serve as a baseline for anomaly detection: messages causing transitions absent from the model are flagged. We implement this principle and evaluate it on a dataset of 230,000 sessions from a SCADA communication protocol captured in a test environment, of which 4,800 sessions contain injected anomalies of five types (replay, truncation, out-of-order, field mutation, and session hijack simulation). The inferred DFA correctly flags anomalous sessions with a precision of 0.91 and a recall of 0.87 averaged across anomaly types. Replay and out-of-order anomalies are detected most reliably; field mutation is detected less well because it does not always alter the message-type sequence. We compare performance to a Hidden Markov Model baseline and a rule-based system, finding the automaton approach superior in precision at comparable recall levels.
